module_title: Transfer of Property Act: Foundational Principles
introduction: This foundational level introduces the Transfer of Property Act (TPA), 1882. It clarifies what exactly constitutes a 'transfer', specifies the types of properties that CANNOT be transferred, and explains the rules regarding transferring property to someone who isn't even born yet.

core_concepts.title: What is a Transfer of Property? (Section 5)
core_concepts.description:
The TPA governs transfers strictly 'Inter Vivos' (between living persons).
- Definition: An act by which a living person conveys property, in present or in future, to one or more other living persons, or to himself.
- 'Living Person' includes: A company, an association, or a body of individuals (whether incorporated or not).
- Exclusions: TPA does NOT cover transfers by operation of law (like inheritance, insolvency, or execution of a court decree) or testamentary succession (Wills). Wills are governed by the Indian Succession Act.

core_concepts.title: What CANNOT be Transferred? (Section 6)
core_concepts.description:
General Rule: Property of any kind may be transferred. However, Section 6 lists strict exceptions:
1. Spes Successionis [Sec 6(a)]: The mere 'chance' of an heir succeeding to an estate cannot be transferred. (e.g., A expects to inherit his father's house. A cannot sell this 'expectation' to B while the father is still alive).
2. Right of Re-entry [Sec 6(b)]: A mere right to re-enter a property for breach of a condition cannot be transferred to anyone except the owner of the property.
3. Easements [Sec 6(c)]: An easement (like a right of way) cannot be transferred apart from the dominant heritage (the land it benefits).
4. Personal Rights [Sec 6(d) & (dd)]: Rights restricted to a person personally (like a right to future maintenance or a personal religious office) cannot be transferred.
5. Mere Right to Sue [Sec 6(e)]: You cannot transfer the right to sue someone for damages.

core_concepts.title: Transfer to an Unborn Person (Section 13)
core_concepts.description:
Property cannot be transferred DIRECTLY to an unborn person. A property must always have an owner; it cannot remain in abeyance.
- The Mechanism: To transfer property to an unborn child, you must first create a 'Prior Life Interest' in favor of a living person. The property vests in the unborn child the moment they are born, though they only gain possession after the life interest holder dies.

core_concepts.title: Rule Against Perpetuity (Section 14)
core_concepts.description:
The law hates tying up property forever (in perpetuity).
- The Rule: You cannot postpone the vesting of property beyond the lifetime of living persons (prior interest holders) plus the minority (18 years) of the ultimate unborn beneficiary. 
- Maximum limit: Life in being + 18 years. Any condition delaying it further (e.g., 'to my unborn grandson when he turns 25') makes the transfer void.

important_entities.name: Spes Successionis
important_entities.key_fact: A mere hope of succession is NOT property.
important_entities.significance: This is heavily tested in CLAT and Judiciary. Transferring a 'chance' of getting property is void ab initio. The law considers it akin to gambling. You cannot sell what you do not presently own.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If a question asks: 'A transfers his property to B through a Will. Is this governed by Section 5 of the TPA?' The answer is **NO**. Section 5 explicitly limits the TPA to transfers between *living persons*. A Will only takes effect after death, hence it is governed by the Indian Succession Act, not the TPA.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: S E R P (Spes successionis, Easement alone, Right to sue, Personal rights)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use SERP to remember the absolute prohibitions on property transfer.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever an exam asks 'What is the maximum time property vesting can be postponed under Section 14?', unconditionally select **Lifetime of prior interest holder + Minority (18 years) of the ultimate beneficiary**.
